title: Quantifying Market Power and Business Dynamism in the Macroeconomy
what_was_fetched: Full PDF (Minneapolis Fed Staff Report 688, sr688.pdf, 70 pages including online appendix) fetched directly from the Fed's own landing-page link and read in full, including abstract, introduction, the three-channel decomposition discussion, and the appendix wedge/robustness sections.
verdict: NEW research/de-loecker-eeckhout-mongey-market-power-dynamism (or equivalent slug) — the paper is a distinct, structurally different exercise from the QJE 2020 paper (De Loecker, Eeckhout & Unger), not a restatement of it, with its own quantified headline results; ENRICH people/jan-eeckhout.md and research/de-loecker-eeckhout-unger-markups.md with cross-links once the new page exists.
claim_grade: A/B — Tier 1 (Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis staff report; authors De Loecker, Eeckhout and Mongey are established academics with a peer-reviewed body of work on this exact topic). Primary source, read directly, not secondary-sourced.
content_summary: De Loecker (KU Leuven), Eeckhout (UPF Barcelona) and Simon Mongey (Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis), 'Quantifying Market Power and Business Dynamism in the Macroeconomy,' Minneapolis Fed Staff Report 688, dated September 4, 2026 (DOI 10.21034/sr.688). Unlike the reduced-form firm-level markup accounting of De Loecker, Eeckhout & Unger (2020, QJE), this paper builds a general-equilibrium model with firm heterogeneity, Cournot oligopoly, and endogenous entry, and structurally estimates it year-by-year on 1980–2023 US data. It decomposes the rise in market power into three channels: (i) the firm productivity distribution, (ii) the composition of overhead vs. variable costs, and (iii) the number of potential competitors (entry conditions). Headline finding: all three channels are necessary — none alone fits the joint data on markups, cost structure, and business dynamism (employment reallocation rate). Quantified welfare results: the net effect of the identified 1980–2023 changes is a 5% decline in welfare and a 6% decline in output; gross output gains of +15.5% from reallocation toward more productive firms are more than offset by labor tied up in fixed/overhead costs and deadweight loss from rising markups. The paper explicitly attributes declining business dynamism (per Decker, Haltiwanger, Jarmin & Miranda 2020) to technology and competition effects working in opposite directions, with competition effects (fewer potential entrants, tougher entry) dominating; rising markups are attributed to both higher fixed costs and fewer potential entrants acting together. Mechanically, market structure changes can arise from 'a reduction in entry through entry barriers' — the paper's only use of that phrase is a generic theoretical mechanism list, not an empirical land/regulatory-barrier finding. A full-text keyword check found zero occurrences of 'land' and zero of 'rent-seeking' anywhere in the 70-page document (including the appendix): the paper is entirely silent on land, real estate, or location as a source of the market power or entry barriers it models — same limitation the wiki's existing De Loecker/Eeckhout/Unger page already notes for the 2020 paper. Robustness: the authors report the core findings hold under Bertrand competition and cost-weighted-markup alternative specifications (appendix).
existing_wiki_coverage: Deep existing coverage of this author team: research/de-loecker-eeckhout-unger-markups.md (Tier: Core, the 2020 QJE paper, extensively mined including a hosted figure, the Traina/Basu/Benkard-Miller-Yurukoglu measurement disputes, and a 2025 reply exchange) and people/jan-eeckhout.md (biography plus a Profit Paradox summary), both last reviewed mid-2026. Neither page currently covers this September 2026 staff report. concepts/superstar-firms and problems/corporate-profits-increasingly-rents also sit in the same citation cluster and would want a cross-link once the new page exists.
uncertainties: This report is a September 2026 staff report, not yet peer-reviewed/journal-published (unlike the 2020 QJE paper); it should be sourced and framed as a working paper, not as a settled peer-reviewed finding, and the existing Nuances-and-Limits pattern (Traina/Basu-style measurement pushback) has not yet had time to develop for this specific paper — none was found because none exists yet. The appendix's per-year wedge decomposition (Figure E1/E2 in the online appendix) was located but not transcribed in full numeric detail; a T1/T2 writer should pull the specific wedge magnitudes (productivity, selection, overhead, markup, misallocation) directly from the appendix figures/tables rather than from this summary alone. The relationship between this GE structural estimate and the QJE reduced-form estimate (e.g., whether markup levels/endpoints match) was not cross-checked line-by-line.

title: Wyoming lawmakers change course on property tax reform amid signs of waning support
what_was_fetched: Full article HTML fetched directly (200 OK, no paywall encountered) and parsed to plain text; read in full including reader comments.
verdict: NEW places/wyoming.md (stub) — the wiki has zero Wyoming coverage and this is a substantive, citable statehouse-reporting case of a property-tax-repeal effort losing momentum, the mirror image of the wiki's split-rate/LVT-enablement coverage. Cross-link from events/2026-state-lvt-enablement-wave.md's 'What Enablement Does' comparative framing if that page is later revised, and from any US property-tax-cap/anti-LVT objections material.
claim_grade: B/C for the reporter's synthesis and framing (Tier 2 — serious statehouse journalism, reliable for votes/figures/quotes but not peer-reviewed); A for the specific named votes, figures and named officials' own statements, which are directly reportable facts (roll-call vote, agency-reported percentage, named legislators' public actions) rather than analysis.
content_summary: Maggie Mullen, WyoFile, published ~September 2026 (dateline not stated in the fetched text beyond 'Sunday' framing and comment dates through Sept. 8, 2026). Wyoming's Joint Revenue Committee voted 7-6 (one excused) NOT to sponsor a bill that would have let voters amend the Wyoming Constitution to eliminate property taxes altogether (a companion bill would have raised sales taxes to backfill the revenue loss); the committee had backed the same measure the prior year. Five of the six 'aye' votes were cast by legislators who had since lost their 2026 reelection bids (named: Sen. Bob Ide and Reps. Gary Brown, Jayme Lien, Robert Wharff, and Tony Locke, all Republicans) — the article frames voters' rejection of Freedom-Caucus-aligned candidates as a signal of waning support for the repeal push; Ide, who originated the repeal idea in 2025, is quoted at the meeting. Separately, the Department of Revenue told the committee that only about 44% of eligible homeowners applied for a 25% residential property-tax exemption Wyoming enacted in 2025 (automatic in its first year, but requiring an application starting in 2026) — reported as new data released alongside the vote. On Nov. 3, 2026, voters face a citizen-initiated ballot measure deciding whether to create a separate 50% residential exemption (on top of/replacing the existing 25% one; the article does not fully spell out whether the two stack). The committee tabled three other property-tax bills until a November meeting (Nov. 19-20), and did vote to sponsor a different bill that would separate residential property in state law and lower its assessment rate from 9.5% to 8.3%. Property taxes in Wyoming fund only local services (education, law enforcement, libraries, water/sewer), not state government; the article states municipalities 'reported making cuts to various services' following the tax cuts, and references Natrona County homeowners who urged the committee last year to skip further cuts citing service impacts, but does not itemize which services were cut or by how much in named budgets (a reader comment, not the reporter, offers unverified specifics about Casper park-maintenance and school-budget cuts — not usable as sourced fact). The 2024 voter-approved constitutional amendment that segregated residential from commercial/agricultural property for tax purposes is the legal predicate the 2026 repeal bill would have built on.
existing_wiki_coverage: None. No Wyoming page, and no existing wiki content on property-tax-repeal/anti-LVT ballot measures of this kind (the wiki's existing US property-tax-cap material, if any, was not separately checked beyond confirming no Wyoming-specific page exists).
uncertainties: The article does not state its own exact publication date in the fetched text (only inferable from context as on or shortly before Sept. 21-22, 2026, given comments through Sept. 8 and forward references to a Nov. 3 election and Nov. 19-20 committee meeting). The relationship between the existing 25% exemption and the Nov. 3 ballot's proposed 50% exemption (replacement vs. additive) is not fully spelled out in the fetched text and should be confirmed against the actual ballot-measure language before a wiki page states it either way. Reported 'service cuts' are asserted by the reporter in general terms without a specific itemized source; a T1 should decide whether to cite this as reported-but-unspecified or seek the underlying municipal reports. No independent Tier 1 (academic/official) source on Wyoming's repeal effort was located or sought in this pass; this brief rests on the single WyoFile article as instructed.

title: Kentucky Can Reform Property Taxes While Protecting Residents, Schools and Other Public Services
what_was_fetched: Full article HTML fetched directly (200 OK) and parsed to plain text; read in full including the visible footnote text at the article's end.
verdict: NEW places/kentucky.md (stub) citing this report as Tier 2 origin/proponent of the anti-cap argument, plus the Kentucky Constitution's fair-cash-value clause as the primary (Tier 1, primary-source) citation; cross-link to the existing events/2026-state-lvt-enablement-wave.md Kentucky section (Louisville split-rate enablement), which this report does not itself address — the two are related but distinct Kentucky property-tax stories (statewide assessment-cap fight vs. Louisville split-rate authorization) and should not be conflated on one page section without distinguishing them.
claim_grade: C for the report's own policy argument and framing (Tier 2 — state policy institute, usable as origin/proponent of the anti-cap position, never as proof the position is correct); the constitutional fair-cash-value requirement itself, if a wiki page states it, needs primary-source verification against the Kentucky Constitution's actual text/section number rather than resting on this report's paraphrase alone (see uncertainties).
content_summary: Jason Bailey and Dustin Pugel, Kentucky Center for Economic Policy (KyPolicy), undated (September 2026 per queue context; not independently confirmed in the fetched text). The report argues against pending Frankfort proposals to cap or freeze property-tax assessments for seniors (e.g., freezing assessed value at age 65, or capping annual assessment increases at 3%), on the grounds that the Kentucky Constitution 'requires all property to be assessed for tax purposes at its fair cash value, "estimated at the price it would bring at a fair voluntary sale"' — meaning any assessment cap or freeze requires a constitutional amendment. The report's substantive argument: caps/freezes favor places and owners where property values (and wealth) are rising over places/owners where they are stagnant, shifting tax burden onto those least able to pay, and disproportionately favor wealthier over working-class families since the dollar value of a frozen assessment's benefit scales with home value. It cites Kentucky-specific figures (from the authors' own analysis of 2024 Census ACS data, not third-party research): 432,000 Kentucky senior homeowners, 69% of whom are 70+ and 22% 80+; the median first-time homebuyer nationally is now 40 (vs. 28 in 1991), meaning a senior freeze shifts costs onto working-age, child-rearing households. It also describes Kentucky's existing HB 44 revenue-cap law (state and local real-property tax rates capped to generate no more than 4% more revenue than the prior year; a hard cap for the state rate, a voter-recall trigger for local rates that would exceed it), arguing this already limits windfall revenue growth from rising assessments, undercutting the case that assessment increases alone drive runaway tax bills. As alternatives, the report recommends a income-based property-tax circuit-breaker program (Kentucky is one of only five states without one) and a senior property-tax deferral program (available in other states), plus administrative modernization (quarterly payment plans, more frequent reassessment to avoid value-spike shocks).
existing_wiki_coverage: events/2026-state-lvt-enablement-wave.md covers a different April 2026 Kentucky action (HB 607, Louisville Metro's split-rate authorization under the Urban Services District) in detail, including the subsequent August 2026 Louisville Metro Council ordinance. No wiki page covers Kentucky's separate, statewide assessment-cap/circuit-breaker debate that this report addresses, and there is no places/kentucky.md jurisdiction-profile page at all.
uncertainties: The report's own footnotes (as fetched) cite only the authors' own analysis of 2024 Census ACS/PUMS data — no Lincoln Institute, IAAO, or peer-reviewed academic source was found cited anywhere in the accessible text, despite a full read; if the live page carries footnote links not rendered in this text extraction (e.g. hover-linked citations), a T1 should re-check the rendered page directly rather than assume this list is exhaustive. The Kentucky Constitution's fair-cash-value requirement is quoted by the report but the specific constitutional section number was not stated in the fetched text and was not independently verified against the Kentucky Constitution's own text in this pass — do not publish a specific section citation (e.g. 'Section 172') without confirming it against the primary constitutional text. The report's publication date was not confirmed beyond the queue's September 2026 attribution.

title: Lessons from South Korea on rent-seeking and growth
what_was_fetched: Full article HTML fetched directly (200 OK; page marked PREMIUM but full text rendered without a login wall in the fetched HTML) and parsed to plain text; read in full.
verdict: REJECT as a citable source — Cachalia is Tier 3 (the byline itself states he is 'a business person and management consultant, is a former DA MP and public enterprises spokesperson,' an op-ed columnist, not an economist), and the piece is an unsourced opinion synthesis with no citations of its own (no paper titles, no data sources for its GDP-per-capita figures, no citation for the Zondo Commission or CPI-score claims beyond bare assertion). Flag only: the piece names political economist Mushtaq Khan as the framework it is applying ('rents attached to productive activity' vs. rents that reward political control), and the wiki currently has no page on Khan or his political-settlements/rents framework — that is a genuine discovery lead for a future, separate acquisition of Khan's own peer-reviewed work, not something this op-ed itself can be cited for. Do not cite this op-ed on places/south-africa.md or concepts/rent-seeking.md.
claim_grade: D — Tier 3 op-ed columnist, no citations of its own, not independently verified against any primary source in this pass.
content_summary: Ghaleb Cachalia, Business Day (South Africa), September 21, 2026. Argues South Africa's stalled post-apartheid development is better explained by what rents were 'expected to produce' than by corruption per se, contrasting South Korea (rents tied to export competitiveness under Park Chung-hee, still corrupt but productive) with Ghana (comparable income at independence, now $36,000 vs. $3,300 GDP per capita — figures given without a cited source) using Mushtaq Khan's framework distinguishing rents attached to productive activity from rents that reward political control (citing Mobutu's Zaire and Nigeria's oil 'paradox of plenty' as Khan's examples, per the op-ed's paraphrase, not a direct quotation from Khan). Applies this to South Africa: mineral rights on the Witwatersrand and in Kimberley were 'consolidated into vertically integrated houses' keeping benefit concentrated within a small number of families across generations; pass laws and the migrant-labour system manufactured cheap, controllable mine labor while gold/diamond exports funded apartheid's fiscus; the Zondo Commission's state-capture findings show the same underlying pattern of political access being more profitable than productive investment, now via post-apartheid procurement/appointments/SOE capture. Cites South Africa's Corruption Perceptions Index score of 41 (vs. a global average of 43) without a source. No footnotes, endnotes, or hyperlinked sources appear anywhere in the piece.
existing_wiki_coverage: places/south-africa.md is substantial (site-value-rating history, Katz Commission, Gaffney's Johannesburg/Cape Town case) but has no coverage of mineral-rights consolidation, pass laws, or the Zondo Commission, and no Mushtaq Khan material anywhere on the wiki. concepts/rent-seeking.md is extensive (Tullock/Krueger origin, multiple 2025-26 empirical papers) but likewise has no Khan entry.
uncertainties: Khan's own notability/tier was not independently assessed against sources/audit/people-tiers.json (he is absent from that file) — he is a SOAS political economist with a substantial peer-reviewed and institutional (DFID/World Bank-adjacent) body of work on rents and political settlements, which would likely qualify him as Tier 1 under the EDITORIAL §4c rubric ('established academics with a peer-reviewed body of work on the topic'), but that determination and the identification of a specific citable Khan paper were not made in this pass — flagging for a future queue item, not resolving here. None of the op-ed's specific factual claims (GDP figures, CPI score, the Witwatersrand/Kimberley consolidation narrative) were cross-checked against a primary or Tier 1 source in this pass.

title: The Contribution of Value Capture from Tax Increment Financing to the Value of Public Service Obligations
what_was_fetched: OJS landing page fetched directly (English abstract available there); the actual article PDF was not at the first-guessed URL (that returned an HTML viewer wrapper) but was located inside that wrapper's embedded download link and fetched successfully as an 11-page PDF, then read in full with PyMuPDF (English abstract plus Indonesian-language body, tables and results sections).
verdict: NEW research page as a short stub, Supplementary tier, with the venue mismatch stated plainly in the page's own text (per EDITORIAL's D-grade-venue-summarised-with-status-stated rule) — OR, T1's likely better call given the thinness of the venue: fold the quantified figures into research/danandjojo-jakarta-lvc-governance.md as a data point on a different, complementary Jakarta rail LVC project, cross-linked, rather than standing up a new page for a single SINTA-indexed civil-engineering-adjacent journal article. Do not present this as equivalent-strength evidence alongside the wiki's peer-reviewed LVC literature.
claim_grade: C — Tier 2/Supplementary. Jurnal Media Teknologi (Universitas Galuh) is a general 'media technology' journal, not an urban-economics, public-finance or transport-economics venue; the paper is co-authored by a doctoral civil-engineering student and a named professor (Universitas Tarumanagara, not the publishing institution), which is itself a venue mismatch the queue flagged correctly. The empirical method (hedonic pricing regression on official NJOP assessed-value data) is standard and legible, but the venue provides no evidence of rigorous economics peer review, and per-cluster regression samples are small (n=30 per station-cluster sub-model).
content_summary: Fery Safaria (Universitas Tarumanagara doctoral civil engineering program) and Carunia Mulya Firdausy, published in Jurnal Media Teknologi Vol. 13 No. 1 (2026), pp. 54-64, DOI 10.25157/jmt.v13i1.6225 (dated 2026-09-16). Studies value capture potential for Jakarta's planned New Jakarta Loopline (NJL) rail line via a tax-increment-financing (TIF) mechanism. Method: Hedonic Pricing Method (HPM) log-linear regression of assessed land value (NJOP, from DKI Jakarta's 2021 tax roll) on distance to station, road width, building-coverage ratio (KLB), plot shape, and a Likert-scaled 'environment' variable, estimated separately per land-use cluster around each of 21 NJL stations; total sample collected was 630 land parcels (within a 500m catchment radius per station), with individual cluster-level regressions run on subsamples as small as 30 (the example residential-cluster model reported: Adjusted R² = 0.782, F = 13.42, n = 30). Value capture (VC) is computed as the simulated post-development NJOP increment per parcel; earmarks are the VC amount assumed fully allocated to infrastructure financing at Jakarta's TIF tax rate of 0.3% (per DKI Jakarta Governor Regulation No. 77/2014). Headline quantified results: projected first-year ridership of 143,022 passengers/day; average PSO (tariff subsidy) of Rp 47,112 per passenger, implying a total first-year PSO subsidy requirement of approximately Rp 2.459 trillion; the computed earmarks value at the 0.3% TIF rate is approximately Rp 514.4 billion — meaning value capture could cover only about 25.13% of the first-year PSO subsidy need if 100% of it were allocated to that purpose. Projecting forward (ridership rising from 183,738/day at 2024 operational start to 323,300/day by 2035, PSO subsidy need rising ~8%/year per the project's pre-feasibility study, and earmarks value tracking the 2015-2021 NJOP growth trend), the paper projects the LVC-TIF earmarks would cover an average of 26.98% of the PSO subsidy need across the concession period. The paper's own conclusion is that LVC-TIF alone is insufficient to replace the PSO tariff subsidy and additional innovative financing is still needed.
existing_wiki_coverage: research/danandjojo-jakarta-lvc-governance.md (Danandjojo, Ramezani & Woltjer 2026) covers a different Jakarta rail project (the MRT) and finds governance fragmentation, not instrument design, is what blocks Jakarta LVC implementation — a natural companion/contrast to this paper's quantified instrument-design finding that even a well-implemented TIF-earmarks scheme would only cover roughly a quarter of the target subsidy. research/rahmawati-indonesia-land-banking-housing.md covers Surabaya land banking, a distinct Indonesian city and mechanism. No existing wiki page covers the New Jakarta Loopline specifically or a NJOP-based hedonic value-capture estimate.
uncertainties: The journal's peer-review rigor and editorial standards were not independently assessed beyond noting the venue/topic mismatch; SINTA/Google Scholar/DOAJ indexing status was not checked. The paper's English abstract is available and was read verbatim, but the full results/discussion is in Indonesian; the figures above were extracted from the Indonesian body text via direct reading (not machine translation) but a native-Indonesian check would be prudent before publishing exact wording. Whether 'Public Service Obligation' subsidy figures in the paper are drawn from a public pre-feasibility ('Pra-FS Konsorsium') document that a T1 could independently verify was not checked — that document is cited by the paper but was not itself located or fetched in this pass. The relationship between the reported 630-parcel total sample and the smaller (n=30) per-cluster regression subsamples should be stated carefully in any wiki text to avoid implying the headline hedonic model itself rests on only 30 observations economy-wide.
